extraction.name: Leaming Multiple La y ers of F eatures from Tin y Images
extraction.description: This work describes how to train a multi-layer generative model of natural images using a dataset of millions of tiny color images. It also details the creation of two reliable labeled subsets, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, for object recognition experiments, demonstrating improved object recognition by pre-training features on unlabeled tiny images.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.citeAs: Alex Krizhevsky. Leaming Multiple La y ers of F eatures from Tin y Images. April 8, 2009.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The base 'tiny images dataset' was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over six months by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using search engines like Google, Flickr, and Altavista. Roughly the first 3000 results for each search term were kept. Perfect duplicates and images with excessive white pixels (synthetic figures) were removed. The dataset contains 80 million color images, downscaled to 32x32, across 79000 search terms. A subset of about 2 million images was used for unsupervised learning experiments. The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets were created by paying students to label subsets of the tiny images dataset. For CIFAR-10, 6000 images per class for 10 classes were collected. For CIFAR-100, 600 images per class for 100 classes were collected. Labelers filtered out mislabeled images based on search terms and their hyponyms, following specific criteria for photo-realism, single prominent object, and clear identity despite occlusion. Duplicate images were removed using L2 norm comparison.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data for the 'tiny images dataset' consists of millions of tiny color images collected from the web using search engines (Google, Flickr, Altavista) based on non-abstract English nouns from the WordNet lexical database. The raw images were then downscaled to 32x32 pixels.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The 'tiny images dataset' was collected over the span of six months.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The collected images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. Perfect duplicates and images with excessively large portions of white pixels (tending to be synthetic figures) were removed from the 'tiny images dataset'. For the labeled subsets (CIFAR-10/100), duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a liberal rejection threshold to capture perfect duplicates and re-saved JPEGs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data preprocessing steps included ZCA whitening transformation to decorrelate data dimensions and set variance in each dimension to 1. Additionally, some of the least significant directions of variance were removed by setting to zero the entries corresponding to the 1000 smallest principal components in the diagonal matrix D of the whitening transformation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset to create CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Each labeler was assigned a class and asked to examine images found using that class name or its WordNet hyponyms as search terms. Labelers were instructed to filter out mislabeled images based on specific criteria: the class name should be a likely answer to 'What is in this picture?', the image should be photo-realistic (rejecting line drawings/cartoons), contain only one prominent instance of the object, and the object's identity should be clear even if partially occluded or from an unusual viewpoint. The authors personally verified every label submitted. The instruction sheet for labelers is reproduced in Appendix C.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors personally verified every label submitted by the labelers.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each image in the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets received one reliable class label from human annotators.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Students were paid a fixed sum per hour spent labeling.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The initial 'tiny images dataset' search term labels are extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The images tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal axes, which is probably caused by the way people take photographs (making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The initial 'tiny images dataset' has no reliable class labels, making it hard to use for object recognition experiments without further annotation. The search term labels are extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The CIFAR-100 dataset was only very recently completed at the time of the paper, so experiments were primarily conducted with CIFAR-10.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning. The dataset is used for unsupervised training of deep generative models, object recognition experiments, and pre-training features for classifiers. The CIFAR-10 dataset was divided into a training set (5000 images per class) and a test set. The CIFAR-100 classes can be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10. RBM features are used to initialize and fine-tune feed-forward neural networks.
